issues.legal_issue: The statutory prohibition on coal mining by operators outside the permitted classes is mandatory and bars their extraction of coal.
material_facts: The operators associated with the alleged workers were not among the classes permitted to carry on coal mining.
The materials before the Court showed no lawful sanction for the mining operations, and the statutory scheme made contravention punishable.
issues.conclusion: The prohibition is peremptory and mandatory, and operators outside the permitted classes cannot extract coal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation Amendment) Act, 1976 expressly prohibited coal mining by persons outside the specified classes; Section 4 made contravention punishable with imprisonment. The Court treated the prohibition as part of a public-interest policy for conserving a vital national resource and planning its use.

predicates.coal_mining_prohibition_case: The proceeding concerns whether coal mining may be carried on despite a statutory prohibition.
predicates.operator_outside_permitted_classes: The operator does not belong to a class legally permitted to carry on the mining activity.
predicates.coal_extraction_is_sought: The operator or another person seeks to extract coal from the mine.
predicates.unauthorized_coal_extraction_is_prohibit: Coal extraction by an operator outside the permitted classes is not allowed.

issues.definition: When a case concerns a statutory prohibition on coal mining, an operator outside the permitted classes cannot extract coal.

issues.legal_issue: Workers have no fundamental right to work in a mine whose operation is unlawful.
material_facts: The alleged employers were not shown to be authorized operators under the statutory scheme.
The mines were not shown to have lawful sanction for operation, and the Court found the operations, if any, to be illicit.
The workers claimed a right to work in the mines despite the prohibition on their operation.
issues.conclusion: Workers, whether genuine or otherwise, cannot claim a fundamental right to work in mines that cannot lawfully be operated.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation Amendment) Act, 1976 prohibited mining except by specified operators, and Section 4 provided a penalty for breach. Because the operations were unlawful, the Court held that workers could not claim a fundamental right to continue them.

predicates.workmen_claim_employment_right: Workers claim a right to continue working at a mine.
predicates.mine_operation_is_unlawful: The mine is being operated without lawful authority.
predicates.operator_outside_permitted_classes: The operator does not belong to a class legally permitted to carry on the mining activity.
predicates.workmen_have_no_fundamental_right_to_wor: Workers have no fundamental right to work in a mine that cannot lawfully be operated.

issues.definition: Workers claiming continued employment at an unlawfully operated mine have no fundamental right to work there when its operator is outside the legally permitted classes.

issues.legal_issue: A private operator cannot claim deemed custodianship of a coal mine without the required governmental notification.
material_facts: The private managements claimed they were deemed custodians operating on behalf of the Central Government.
No notification authorizing the relevant taking over of management or establishing custodianship was produced or shown to exist.
The Central Government opposed the mining operations.
issues.conclusion: Without the required notification, a private agency cannot claim actual or deemed custodianship and cannot rely on that status to extract coal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act, 1973 required a written governmental direction for the relevant vesting of rights in a Government company. The Court held that the necessary notification was a sine qua non for actual or deemed custodianship, so a private agency could not assume that status on its own.

predicates.private_operator_claims_custodianship: A private operator asserts that it holds the mine as a custodian on behalf of the government.
predicates.required_written_authorization_is_absent: The written governmental authorization required for that custodianship has not been issued.
predicates.coal_extraction_is_sought: The operator seeks to extract coal from the mine.
predicates.private_operator_cannot_claim_custodians: The private operator cannot rely on claimed custodianship as authority to extract coal.

issues.definition: A private operator seeking to extract coal cannot rely on custodianship when it claims that status but lacks the required written governmental authorization.

issues.legal_issue: The difference in treatment between workers at lawfully operating mines and workers at mines validly closed under a statutory prohibition does not violate equality.
material_facts: The workers argued that employees in nationalized mines received protection and benefits while workers at mines barred from operating were left without them.
The Court concluded that the affected mines had been validly closed and that no one employed there could compel their reopening on grounds of discrimination.
A larger Bench of the Court had already upheld the validity of the statutory scheme.
issues.conclusion: There was no violation of Article 14; workers at validly closed mines could not demand that the mines be reopened on grounds of discrimination, and claims for lay-off or other benefits belonged to a different jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution did not require the reopening of mines validly closed under Section 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation Amendment) Act, 1976. The Court also relied on the binding effect under Article 141 of the earlier larger-Bench decision upholding the statute, holding that a new argument could not undo that precedent.

rule.if: workmen_raise_equality_challenge and affected_mine_is_validly_closed and comparator_mines_are_lawfully_operated and statute_was_previously_upheld_by_larger_bench

predicates.workmen_raise_equality_challenge: Workers challenge their treatment by comparing their position with workers in other mines.
predicates.affected_mine_is_validly_closed: The mine where the workers were employed has been lawfully closed under the applicable prohibition.
predicates.comparator_mines_are_lawfully_operated: The mines used as comparators are permitted to operate lawfully under the applicable scheme.
predicates.statute_was_previously_upheld_by_larger_: A larger bench has already upheld the validity of the statutory scheme.
predicates.different_treatment_does_not_make_the_st: The difference in treatment does not make the valid closure an equality violation.

issues.definition: When workers challenge unequal treatment, a valid closure of their mine does not become an equality violation merely because comparator mines lawfully operate, particularly where a larger bench has already upheld the statutory scheme.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot appoint a receiver or otherwise authorize coal extraction that a mandatory statutory prohibition forbids.
material_facts: Receivers and other court officers had been appointed in some matters, and coal extraction was reportedly continuing under those arrangements.
The statutory prohibition on mining by unauthorized operators was mandatory and punishable.
The Court had upheld the validity of the prohibition.
issues.conclusion: No court may appoint a receiver or otherwise permit coal extraction contrary to the prohibition, and existing interim orders permitting extraction were vacated.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation Amendment) Act, 1976 imposed a mandatory prohibition, and Section 4 made breach punishable. The Court had upheld the statute's constitutionality and held that judicial orders could not authorize conduct the statute prohibited.

predicates.court_receiver_or_permission_case: The proceeding concerns a court-appointed receiver or another judicial authorization relating to mining.
predicates.coal_extraction_is_sought: A receiver, officer, or other person seeks to extract coal from a mine.
predicates.statutory_prohibition_is_mandatory_and_c: A mandatory prohibition on the mining activity has been upheld as constitutionally valid.
predicates.courts_may_not_authorize_prohibited_coal: A court cannot authorize coal extraction that the mandatory prohibition forbids.

issues.definition: In a proceeding about judicial authority over mining, a court cannot authorize coal extraction when a mandatory, constitutionally valid prohibition applies.
